{{nihongo|'''Yoshihisa Yamamoto'''|山本 喜久|Yamamoto Yoshihisa|}} is the director of Physics & Informatics Laboratories (PHI Labs), NTT Research, Inc. He is also Professor (Emeritus) at [[Stanford University]] and [[National Institute of Informatics]] (Tokyo).

== Biography ==
Yamamoto was born in [[Tokyo]] on November 21, 1950. In 1973 he received his B.S. degree from [[Tokyo Institute of Technology]]. He continued his studies at [[the University of Tokyo]] where he received his M.S. in 1975 and Ph.D. in 1978. From 1978 to 1992, he worked at NTT [[Basic research|Basic Research]] Laboratories in Tokyo. Since 1992, he has been a professor of applied physics and electrical engineering at [[Stanford University]] in the United States and currently a professor (emeritus). Since 2003, he also has been a professor at [[National Institute of Informatics]] in Tokyo and currently a professor (emeritus). In 2019, he became a founding director of NTT PHI Labs in Silicon Valley, California, the United States.

== Work ==

Yamamoto's scientific focuses in the 1980s were [[fiber-optic communication|coherent optical fiber communications]],<ref name="Santori2002"/> [[optical amplifier]] repeater systems,<ref name="Benson2000"/> photon number squeezing in semiconductor lasers, [[Quantum nondemolition measurement|quantum non-demolition (QND) measurements]] and other experimental and theoretical<ref name="Alter2001"/> [[quantum optics]] subjects. Some of Yamamoto's key works from this era are proposals for how to physically realize photon-number squeezing,<ref name="Yamamoto1986 Machida1987"/> QND measurement,<ref name="Imoto1985"/> and a gate model [[quantum computer]] using single atoms and photons.<ref name="qc1988"/> His most prominent work in the 1990s is in semiconductor [[cavity quantum electrodynamics]]<ref name="Yamamoto book"/> (especially involving microcavities and quantum wells) and quantum transport effects in mesoscopic devices.<ref name="Oliver1999"/>

During the 2000s, his most important work was on the development of optically-active quantum dots as a platform for quantum information processing (both as [[single-photon source]]s <ref name="Santori2002"/><ref name="Benson2000"/> and as hosts for spin qubits.<ref name="Press2008"/><ref name="DeGreve2012"/>) Another important work was on [[Bose–Einstein condensation of polaritons|exciton-polariton condensation]] effects.<ref name="Deng2002"/><ref name="Deng2010"/> Yamamoto was also active in the development of security theory and realization of quantum key distribution protocols.<ref name="Inoue2002"/><ref name="Takesue2007"/> Landmark papers from this era include the demonstration of indistinguishable photons from a single quantum dot;<ref name="Santori2002"/> the proposal for [[biexciton]] cascade emission as a method for generating entangled photons from a single quantum dot <ref name="Benson2000"/> (this is the proposal underlying essentially all QD entangled-photon sources, such as those reviewed in <ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1038/nphoton.2007.46 | volume=1 | issue=4 | title=Semiconductor quantum light sources | year=2007 | journal=Nature Photonics | pages=215–223 | author=Shields Andrew J| arxiv=0704.0403 | bibcode=2007NaPho...1..215S | s2cid=119664751 }}</ref>), and control of a single spin qubit in a quantum dot using optical pulses.<ref name="Press2008"/>

During the 2010s, his work has continued on exploring quantum dots as a platform for building both quantum repeaters and quantum computers. One highlight was the co-first demonstration (with [[Ataç İmamoğlu]]'s group at [[ETH]]) of entanglement between a spin in a quantum dot and a photon emitted by it.<ref name="DeGreve2012"/> Work on [[exciton-polariton]]s continued. Since 2012, Yamamoto has studied the required number of physical qubits and expected computational time in a gate-model fault-tolerant quantum computer <ref name="Jones2012"/> and pioneered the development of a novel quantum/classical hybrid computer, called coherent Ising machine <ref name="McMahon2016"/> inspired by developments in digital coherent optical communications and degenerate [[optical parametric oscillator]]s.

== Awards ==
Yamamoto is a fellow of the [[Optical Society of America]] (now Optica), the [[American Physical Society]], and the [[Japan Society of Applied Physics]]. In 1985, Yamamoto received the Achievement Award of the Institute of Electronics, Information and Communication Engineers (IEICE) of Japan on his early work on coherent optical communications. In 1992, he received the  [[Nishina Memorial Prize|Nishina Prize]]<ref name="Yamamoto Nishina"/> and [[Carl Zeiss Foundation|the Carl Zeiss Award]]<ref name="Yamamoto Carl Zeiss"/> on his pioneering work on squeezed state generation in semiconductor lasers. In 2000, he received [[IEEE|the IEEE LEOS Quantum Electronics Award]]<ref name="Yamamoto IEEE"/> and the Matsuo Science Prize. In 2005, he received [[Medals of Honor (Japan)|the Medal of Honour with Purple Ribbon]] from the Government of Japan.<ref name="Yamamoto Purple Ribbon"/> In 2010, he was the Hermann Anton Haus Lecturer at MIT <ref name="Yamamoto MIT"/> and gave a lecture on exciton-polariton condensation. In 2011, he received the Okawa Prize <ref name="Yamamoto Okawa"/> on his pioneering work on single photon generation from a quantum dot. In 2022, he received the [[Willis Lamb]] Award <ref name="Yamamoto Willis Lamb"/> on his pioneering work on coherent Ising machines.
